📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 21:00 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 08:25 EST, 13 November 2026.

According to recent reports, there are few sights more incendiary to the modern manager than a footballer reaching for his phone as soon as he walks through the dressing room door. So you can imagine the reaction Jake O’Brien received when he pulled out his mobile just before one half-time team talk.

But the Everton and Republic of Ireland defender had a good excuse: he’s the only Type One diabetic playing in the Premier League.

O’Brien’s body is unable to create insulin, the hormone that regulates the amount of glucose in your blood.

Loaded on his mobile is an app linked via Bluetooth to a circular device on his arm which gives a reading of his blood sugar levels. It is then that he takes out a needle and injects the necessary insulin dose into his thigh or stomach.

It has been revealed that ‘There was one guy who didn’t react too well. Mentioning no names! He was saying: "What are you doing on your phone?"' O’Brien recalls. ‘But he soon realised what it was for.’.

It can also come as a shock to the uninitiated among his team-mates.

‘One or two are taken aback at first,’ he indicates. ‘It can be a bit confusing. “What’s he doing?’’ Or maybe those that are a little squeamish, but they soon get used to it. It's only a small needle.'.

Everton and Ireland defender Jake O'Brien is the only diabetic footballer in the Premier League.

O'Brien (pictured attending an awareness workshop put on by Everton) revels in the role of being a diabetes ambassador.

O'Brien (pictured with his partner Sophie) claims some of his team-mates are 'taken aback' when he injects himself with insulin (Source: Instagram/Obrienjake_).

Tracking blood glucose levels is now an everyday part of O'Brien's life but it is a life that was unwittingly put in jeopardy prior to his diagnosis at 16.

O’Brien was later told he had been just one day away from slipping into a coma when his concerned parents ushered him to the doctors near the family home in Youghal, County Cork, for a check-up.

Recent findings suggest that their sports-mad son, who had won national titles at boxing and hurling, was tired, losing weight and had an insatiable thirst despite drinking eight to nine litres of water a day. He had lost seven kilograms in just over a week. A blood test revealed his blood sugar was ten times what was considered stable and he was rushed to hospital.

In a recent development, ‘I was told I was a day away from a coma,' says O'Brien. 'If I had gone to sleep that night without having gone to the doctor, who knows?’.

He went into hospital that night weighing 53kg, or just over eight stone. Two weeks post-diagnosis he was back up to 60kg, and within two years he had put on a whopping 30kg.

Sources indicate that 'Yeah, 30kg,' laughs O'Brien. 'I know it's not normal. It must have been some grocery bill for Mum, but I was motivated to put on the weight, going to the gym all the time.

‘I was a bit naive about it all,' he deadpans. ‘I never expected to have anything but once I knew what diabetes was, I didn’t wallow in it, I took it as a positive. Everything just clicked for me physically. I just thought, "Right, now I know what’s wrong, I can get on with my life again".

‘It was a pain going in and out of hospital, but I just took it as education and wanted to get my sport back on track.

It has been revealed that 'My family are... I wouldn't say cold, but matter of fact. Supportive, obviously, but they are all sporty too, so it was just, "Get on with it".'.

O'Brien's life in the Premier League would have seemed inconceivable when he fell down to 53kg as a teenager and was hospitalised.

Sources indicate that he is now an imposing 6ft 6in tall, weighing around 96kg. His physique offers no outward indication of the daily challenge he is dealing with.

Sources indicate that today, relaxing in the cafe at Everton’s Finch Farm training complex, O’Brien is an imposing 6ft 6in tall, weighing around 96kg. His physique offers no outward indication of the daily challenge he is dealing with.

It has been revealed that there’s a Cork-lilt to his softly spoken Irish tone. He’s polite and engaging and it’s clear he revels in the role of being a diabetes ambassador, spreading the message that diagnosis doesn’t have to end your dreams.

Such has been his impact, he has even attracted support from fans of the other club in the city.

One, six-year-old Liverpool fan Louis, reached out via Instagram to ask O’Brien how he kept up his glucose levels during a game and whether he suffered any ‘hypos’ - the expression for hypoglycemic episodes, when the blood sugar drops too low and leaves you faint or dizzy.

Louis, whose siblings Paisley and Evie also have Type One diabetes, followed up by challenging O’Brien to a penalty shootout. If the Everton man lost, he faced a forfeit, he would have to shout ‘Up the Reds’ on social media.

‘You play for the wrong team but you're still a Type One hero, and Mum says you're proof that diabetes doesn't stop you from playing at the top level,’ posted Louis.

Touched by the message, O’Brien asked Everton to invite the youngster and his family to training for a kickabout, although ultimately, we are assured they reached a compromise on the penalties forfeit.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I’ve struck up a rapport with some kids and groups here and in Ireland,' says O'Brien. 'They often have the same story as mine of not being sure what the future holds.

‘There’s a significant misconception about diabetes over what it is and the limitations it brings.

‘Just because you have diabetes doesn’t mean your dreams are over.’.

‘Adrenaline is higher on match days so that can change how you feel. I may inject four times before a night game and a bit more at half-time'.

‘Just because you have diabetes doesn’t mean your dreams are over,’ indicates O'Brien, who also excelled at boxing and hurling as a boy (Source: TikTok/Everton).

The centre back credits boxing for helping discipline with his diet but underlines ‘no food is off limits, it’s just about applying common sense'.

A typical day sees him eat eggs, salmon and dates for breakfast to match his insulin doses to the carbohydrates he’s taking on around 9.30am before training. Afterwards he’ll have a light lunch at 2pm then take something back from the training ground for a light evening meal.

Sources indicate that ‘I just have to watch carbohydrates. I’ll eat more of them on match day but then work out my insulin ratio to the amount I eat and whether I need to inject more.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Adrenaline is higher on match days so that can change how you feel, I may inject four times before a night game and inject a bit more at half-time. If it’s not quite right you may get a bit heavy-legged or if I get a few cramps I may need a gel. But I've had no dangerous episodes.'.

When World Diabetes Day dawns on Saturday, O’Brien will be fully focused on preparing to play for Ireland in Austria in the Nations League.

It will give him a chance to revert to his favoured centre back position having been asked to fill in predominantly at right back under David Moyes.

He acknowledges it's not his preferred role but dismisses rumours that he wanted to leave as a result in the summer.

'There was nothing in that,' O'Brien affirms. ‘I was never close to leaving.

Recent findings suggest that 'People know I'm not a natural right back but I'll play wherever I need to, to help the team. We're only a small squad so it’s crucial everyone chips in.

‘There’s a lot of different right backs. I see Arsenal have centre backs playing at right back so I can take pointers from them but then again, I am 6ft 6in so I’m not the average shape.’.

O'Brien insists there was 'nothing in' reports that he wanted to leave Everton last summer to get more minutes at his preferred position of centre back.

At least O’Brien has former Everton captain Seamus Coleman on hand for advice.

‘Seamus is a good friend. He still gives me pointers of where to be, positioning wise and seeing the game differently.'.

Ireland assistant John O'Shea, a versatile defender himself in his Manchester United days, is another mentor. O’Shea and Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrímsson were at Hill Dickinson Stadium to watch O'Brien play his part in Everton's recent Carabao Cup win over Newcastle.

Recent findings suggest that 'Heimir is a good guy,' states O'Brien. 'Very understanding. It's always a nice change of scenery to link up with Ireland. We've got a difficult couple of games (Austria and Kosovo) but hopefully if we get two wins it’s within reach.'.

Indeed, if there's a mantra that personifies O'Brien's outlook on life, no matter what knocks you take, it is: always believe you can still achieve.

'Don’t be afraid and don’t let anything hold you back, that's what I say.'.

L’ex biancoceleste elogia il gioco di Gattuso e la forza del gruppo, ma indica nella prima sconfitta una prova da superare.

In a recent development, secondo quanto riportato da La Gazzetta dello Sport, Nestor Sensini crede nella possibilità che la Lazio vinca lo scudetto. L’ex biancoceleste considera il titolo una sorta di miracolo sportivo, ma vede nella squadra di Gattuso le condizioni per provarci: «Ha tutte le qualità per centrare l’impresa.» Cita l’ambiente, la grinta e la preparazione tattica dell’allenatore, oltre alla consapevolezza che il gruppo sta acquisendo partita dopo partita.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM.

Il legame di Sensini con la Lazio risale al titolo conquistato in biancoceleste. Pur essendo affezionato anche a Udinese e Parma, ricorda soprattutto la festa vissuta a Roma: «Alla Lazio ho conquistato il mio scudetto. Quell’esperienza si è appiccicata alla pelle, la festa di un popolo intero. Come si fa a dimenticare una cosa così?».

It has been revealed that per Sensini, il gioco è uno dei punti di forza della Lazio. Gattuso ha dato alla squadra un’identità precisa: sa difendere e attaccare coinvolgendo l’intero organico. L’ex calciatore attribuisce questo risultato alla capacità del tecnico di convincere tutti della validità delle proprie idee.

Richiamando la sua esperienza in diversi spogliatoi, anche in quelli dove giocava Maradona, Sensini osserva che può esserci qualche scontento perfino quando arrivano i risultati. Alla Lazio, invece, gli sembra di vedere un gruppo unito, senza prime donne né i fuoriclasse della squadra con cui vinse lo scudetto, ma disposto a lavorare per un obiettivo comune. «In questa squadra vedo il carattere del suo allenatore», dice.

Tra i singoli cita Zaccagni, Noslin e Frattesi, pur insistendo sul collettivo e sulla disponibilità a fare una corsa in più per aiutare un compagno in difficoltà.

Industry observers note that sensini riconosce che Inter e Roma hanno rose superiori per qualità e quantità e che i mezzi finanziari della Lazio non sono paragonabili a quelli degli altri club. Per questo fa i complimenti ai tecnici e ai dirigenti che hanno individuato i giocatori adatti al progetto di Gattuso. Ritiene comunque meritata la posizione della Lazio: «Nove vittorie, due pareggi e zero sconfitte: il cammino è fantastico.».

In a recent development, il suo dubbio riguarda la risposta della squadra a un risultato negativo: «Prima o poi arriverà una sconfitta e bisognerà vedere come il gruppo reagirà alla caduta.» Sensini è convinto che Gattuso saprà affrontare anche quei momenti, purché l’ambiente resti vicino ai giocatori. Sulla corsa al titolo si sbilancia: «Lo stesso dovranno fare i suoi giocatori, e mi sbilancio: alla fine, ce la faranno. E io sarò a festeggiare con loro».

Gasly takes shock Italian GP pole and denies Russell

📅 05 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources.
  • It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sometimes inspiration can come from the unlikeliest of sources. After claiming the first pole of his Formula One career, an absolutely stunning effort in his 192nd attempt – edging out Mercedes’ George Russell right at the death – Alpine’s Pierre Gasly revealed that a harmless jibe from his performance coach Ben Thorpe just before the session started had riled him up.

It turned out Gasly and Russell had been playing online chess until about 15 minutes before qualifying.

Recent findings suggest that “Since the [drivers’] briefing last night, I figured out that he [Russell] is obsessed with chess, and so am I,” Gasly explained later in his press conference. “There are a few of us in the paddock who are. So we have exchanged our IDs on Chess.com and we have had a little game going on.

It has been revealed that “I won yesterday, and another one that carried on into today,” the Frenchman added. “I was feeling confident and I was picking [taking] piece after piece. Then Ben told me: ‘You are getting George here but he is going to get you in a few minutes!’. And I thought ‘F--- off!’.”.

What a way to break your duck. And what a day on which to do it. On Friday, Gasly lost his only podium of the season when the International Court of Appeal reinstated two five-second penalties he received in Monaco, dropping him from third to seventh in that race. The ruling produced fireworks when Flavio Briatore, Alpine’s executive adviser, then accused one of the judges on the ICA panel of being biased towards McLaren, one of two teams who had brought the appeal.

Sources indicate that another 24 hours later, the fireworks were for all the right reasons. And there was no appealing the result; the start of Russell’s final lap in Q3 was slightly compromised by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, but the Englishman could have no real complaints, losing out by 0.060secs in the end, prompting wild celebrations in the Alpine garage.

To say the result was a surprise would be an understatement. This was the Enstone team’s first pole in 17 years, since Fernando Alonso took P1 Renault at the 2009 Hungarian Grand Prix.

The warning signs were there. Alpine had been quick all weekend. But the Tifosi packing Monza’s grandstands fully expected it to be a battle between Mercedes and their beloved Ferrari for pole.

The Scuderia’s performance was underwhelming. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were only ninth and 10th quickest in Q2, the latter squeaking into Q3 by one thousandth of a second from Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto. “F--- me,” Hamilton noted after dodging that bullet.

It has been revealed that and although they improved a bit in Q3, Hamilton managing to claim P5, just behind Leclerc in P4, they never threatened the front row. In fact, they later got lucky as McLaren’s Oscar Piastri, who took P3, was later hit with a three-place grid drop post-qualifying for impeding Liam Lawson, meaning both Ferrari drivers rose one place.

In a recent development, it could prove significant. Hamilton, like Russell, knows this weekend represents a golden opportunity to close the gap to Kimi Antonelli in the title race. The two Britons are tied second in the championship heading into the weekend, 59 points behind the Italian. But Antonelli, who sacrificed his qualifying to help Russell, must start from the back of the grid on Sunday due to exceeding the permitted number of engines in a season.

In a recent development, it promises to be a fascinating race, with Antonelli fighting his way through the pack and Russell and Hamilton trying to make hay while they can. Russell sounded confident. “I think they [Alpine] have got a car that’s got some good straight-line speed, which will be nice for them in the race. But, yeah, confident I’ve got the pace to go for the win.”.

Could he be underestimating Gasly again? The Frenchman, who lives locally in Milan and speaks fluent Italian, has won here before. He claimed the only victory of his F1 career at Monza for AlphaTauri in 2020.

Industry observers note that “Anything is possible tomorrow,” insisted Steve Nielsen, Alpine’s managing director. “We didn’t expect to be in pole position, we are. Tomorrow, good starts, good strategy, good pit stops – who knows? Let’s try to win it.”.

It has been revealed that gasly himself mentioned he had no idea what he was capable of. “My initiative is to stay first as long as I can. How long is that going to be? I have no idea. My focus is going to be on my driving and making no mistakes and making the best out of what I have.” Perhaps that will be enough for another checkmate.

Antonelli acknowledged that his engine-parts grid penalty meant he had no reason not to assist his teamate Russell by offering towing assistance.

He seemed a little peeved at times on the radio, but he did his job. With Russell likely to need to return the favour for him later this season, there is no point causing bother.

Sources indicate that he told Sky Sports: “It’s what I have to do. The team asked me and of course I did what I had to do, I tried to help as much as possible. It’s a bit weird going in two, even the lap I did alone was a bit of a weird feeling. Overall with the penalty today I had to be a good teammate and I had to help as much as I could. I think I did a good job with that and happy it worked out.”.

Here’s Oscar Piastri, asked if a pole had been possible: “I don’t think so, no. I think the first lap felt good and I tried to see if anyone wanted to go in front out of the pit lane but no one did and I knew it was always going to be difficult and misjudged the braking a little bit and locked up. That was the session but good to have a decent result, it has been a while. I’ll take it.”.

Alpine managing director Steve Nielsen remarked to Sky Sports that they were aiming high: “Pierre is a class act, as you say, if you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year. We haven’t always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have he has delivered. Particularly earlier in the season so to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful.

In a recent development, “We mustn’t forget Franco either, he’s done a great job today. I really feel we have given them a good car, and who knows? Anything is possible tomorrow.”.

Here’s what he noted immediately after the session: “Massive congrats to Pierre because that’s an incredible performance. We were actually playing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying and he beat me there and I thought ‘well I think I’ll beat you in qualifying’ and here we are - he’s ahead of me again! I was disappointed not to get pole. It was a bit messy with Verstappen opening the lap. But Pierre and Alpine have been super fast, even from Q1. Happy to see them get a good result.”.

Gasly’s advantage, it appears, seems to be over Russell’s car understeering and lacking grip in turbulent air.

P1 ☝️#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/U0hebWsjWY.

Industry observers note that he indicates: “It was amazing, thank you everyone. It was an incredible qualy. I felt very good in the car. I was trying to chip away in evert session. I’m so happy, it’s been nine years trying to get a pole. First win [was] in Monza, to get pole is very special.”.

He then pays credit to his team and the fans in Italian, and I am leaning on my Latin to get the gist of it.

“I was disappointed not to get the pole,” admits Russell who mentioned he had been playing chess with Gasly before the game and the Frenchman won that, with Russell confident he was going to beat him in qualifying.

Alpine been in the news all weekend. Fair to say that pole lap from Gasly is better PR for the team than Flavio Briatore’s bizarre outburst in the FIA press conference yesterday. Well done that man.

Recent findings suggest that his tone is evidently disappointed. In truth, given Hamilton is fifth, he is in a strong position to have the best of the weekend.

Gasly, yes, was fastest, but Russell has been the most consistent.

Industry observers note that piastri could be in trouble, too, for impeding earlier in the day’s sesion. Ferrari, in fourth and fifth, do not look entirely competitive.

Russell is second, Piastri third, Leclerc fourth, Hamilton fifth, Verstappen sixth, Antonelli seventh, Colapinto eighth, Norris ninth and Lindblad 10th.

According to recent reports, he starts his flying lap, and locks up at turn 1 and exceeds track limits. That means Norris will be unable to get a tow from him too.

After being the quickest at FP2 and FP3, he is top of the pack once more with a bit over five minutes left.

Antonelli has done him a favour there, but Russell may need to return the favour in similar circumstances down the line.

Hamilton is now down in ninth, and struggling, about 0.8s off the pace.

Piastri may be in for some bother.

Sources indicate that hamilton needs to catch Leclerc to get a tow. It failed to happen last time out.

Piastri finished Q2 in P2 but it looks likely he'll be penalised for this incident involving Lawson#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/RGzzEeqyql.

Lawson, Hulkenberg, Sainz, Ocon, Bearman and Bortoleto are all out.

Hamilton is 10th, one-thousandth of a second quick enough to scrape through, and Leclrec ninth.

“**** me” exclaims Hamilton, without saying, ‘Asterisk’ once.

Antonelli asks for the chance to go out with another team ahead so he can get a tow of his own.

Norris now second quickest, so perhaps those brakes are up to speed.

There is some suggestion that Hamilton might need a front wing change.

The Silver Arrows working in tandem Kimi in front, George slipstreaming behind #F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/H476E91GJs.

But Gasly is going fastest in his out lap.

Verstappen now goes fastest. Lawson is in behind, with Carlos Sainz making a surprise appearance up top.

Hamilton and Russell are yet to lay down times.

Norris is uncomfortable with his brakes at Monza.

Given he’s well outside of the fastest for now, the pressure is on him to make Q3.

The two Aston Martins are out, along with Yuki Tsunoda, Alex Albon, Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez.

Q2 awaits, with Gasly fastest - aiming for what would be his first pole.

It has been revealed that alonso, meanwhile, has wirthdrawn from the session. Things going wrong for the veteran, who must have no other hobbies.

Pierre Gasly takes his Alpine for a spin. He is now fastest, with Verstappen second, and Colapinto bookending the Dutchman.

Antonelli and then Russell next, with the stricken Antonelli likely to give his colleague a tow.

The Red Bull man is 0.216s clear of Hamilton, with Piastri just behind.

No surprising stragglers just yet, but 11 minutes to go of this section.

We’ve 16 minutes left, and some cars are finally coming out to do battle.

According to recent reports, 18 minutes ahead before the final two rounds. Nobody is doing anything. As they say in football: tactically fascinating.

According to recent reports, monza paddock is absolutely sweltering. 33.8C out here. I just passed Fabio Capello on my way back to the media centre. He was speaking to Sky Sports Italia so I wasn’t able to give him my thoughts on where he went wrong at the 2010 World Cup.

Decent ding dong between Hamilton and Verstappen in practice earlier. Hopefully Hamilton is fired up for this. With Antonelli taking his grid drop at his home race, there’s a substantial opportunity for both Hamilton and Russell to close the gap this weekend.

The cars will soon be out on the track, and we’ll have reports of their progress.

According to recent reports, the Monegasque (look it up) is the junior partner at this point, whether he wants to be or not. That might not make him entirely delighted, but he can tow the British driver around and give him a launch for fast laps, if he’s feeling helpful.

Everyone now has access to PowerPoint, which means we all now have to have, “learnings.”.

Imagine if someone you met in real life said that to you.

3 hours of laps and learnings done.#ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/GTvOvL5L5M.

Given Antonelli is still one of the quickest on the track, it would be no surprise if he can at least make the top 10.

Favourable accidents and yellow flags might offer up more opportunities, too, but both Hamilton and Russell need to strike while they have such a clear advantage.

George Russell tops Lewis Hamilton in final practice in Monza 🇮🇹💪 pic.twitter.com/jxIO13aRX6.

I’m as massive a fan of F1 as the next man, assuming the next man quite likes F1, but there is something strange about supporting a car organization, isn’t there?

The session starts in around 40 minutes, so drivers are on their Gameboys and Instagram, and reading the weekend edition of The Telegraph.

Words we live by, this weekend and always ❤️ pic.twitter.com/0QoGlpzOHI.

Here’s our interview with Alex Albon about a grim weekend at Monza.

“Alex Albon remembers the 2022 Italian Grand Prix well. He had been looking forward to it. ‘We had a car which was good down the straights that year so I was quite excited to be going to Monza,” the Williams driver recalls, a little wistfully.

‘We did FP1 and FP2 and sure enough we were quick so I was like: ‘This is going to be a good weekend.’.

“Albon could not have been more wrong. He remembers waking at around 1am that night and being unable to get back to sleep.

According to recent reports, “What happened next was the stuff of nightmares. Albon called the doctor, was diagnosed with appendicitis, sent to San Gerardo Hospital in Monza for surgery, only to suffer an unexpected complication during the procedure, which resulted in acute respiratory failure.”.

He shares the joint record with Michael Schumacher for most wins at Monza.

It has been revealed that schumacher, a Ferrari legend, ended his career with five. Hamilton has the same.

Sport loves an emotional link to records, so be prepared for this to become a massive moment.

Five wins apiece for Michael and Lewis 🖐#F1 #ItalianGP pic.twitter.com/j10lMygYft.

The Italian team are bringing an upgrade engine to Monza for the weekend.

Hamilton would desperately love to go out at the top after what is a remarkable return to decent form after some years of desperate struggle.

With Antonelli possibly out of the running this weekend, this is the chance to change the - *spits in self-scorn* - narrative.

Russell might have incurred a penalty if he had done this in qualifying.

The Mercedes man blocked Oscar Piastri’s run at a corner, forcing some heavy braking from his rival.

Thankfully, Piastri ducked out, and thankfully for Russell, he’s not facing censure.

The pair are just natural friends.

Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton go racing! 🍿 pic.twitter.com/Zs8u8h4XoT.

The former world champion is still looking for more from his car.

“Just looking at the deltas there, I was losing something like 0.6secs to George on the straights, which is something we need to look into,” Hamilton remarked yesterday, before explaining his conundrum for qualifying, suggesting he may go out after Leclerc.

“The tow is everything here so [I’m] likely to be looking for the tow.”.

Because Antonelli exceeded the limit of parts used for his engine, he is taking a grid penalty at Monza.

Few would entirely rule out a storming ride for him on Sunday to end up top of the pack, but is is clearly a huge task for him to score points of any kind with that disadvantage.

They are now likely both past their peaks, but Hamilton and Verstappen recalled their battles of 2021 when they clashed in practice earlier.

Verstappen was already hacked off with Hamilton for seemingly obstructing his path earlier in the session, and they almost came together in the dying moments of the session.

Hamilton needed to take the escape road at the first chicane, where the pair made contact in 2021, as Verstappen looked to slip around his occasional rival. The two of them scarcely avoided another contact.

On the radios, Verstappen claimed, “He caused that,” while Hamilton reported to Ferrari that he was, “Blocked by Max.” Perhaps there will be more aggro later.

The full list of times from earlier today.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of and qualifying for the Monza Grand Prix.

Before the weekend’s racing, George Russell was, at least publicly, less than bullish about his chances in Italy.

He did, though, believe he would deliver a better showing than he had in recent weeks.

“I don’t know if we can say we’re favourites this weekend, but we probably have a greater opportunity than we’ve had in the last two races where it’s been less about the power unit and more about the chassis,” he noted.

It has been revealed that “It’s so close right now, that last tenth in qualifying can be the difference of a couple of positions, which can change the podium. Right now, I don’t know who is going to be the team to beat.”.

According to recent reports, russell was almost a minute off winner Lando Norris of McLaren in Hungary, finishing seventh in his Mercedes. Two weeks ago, in the Netherlands, he took the last spot on the podium, with Norris winning again.

However, in the second practice session on Friday and FP3 today, Russell was quickest. He led his former colleague, Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who was second fastest.

Red Bull’s Max Verstappen hinted at a rare good weekend as he was third fastest, about a third of a second behind Russell.

Russell, of course, needs a win soon, or he is in danger of seeing the championship run away from him entirely, as Kimi Antonelli already leads him by 59 points in the world title chase.

Industry observers note that perhaps psychologically just as pressing is that erstwhile teammate Hamilton is tied with Russell on 183 points, in third because he has one victory compared to Russell’s two. Slipping down the rankings could knock his confidence.

Russell has not secured pole for the last four races, so a strong showing in qualifying might be the boost he needs ahead of Sunday’s race, while Norris is looking for a pole position hat-trick.

It has been revealed that bayern Munich’s Harry Kane became the first Bundesliga player to win the Ballon d’Or in 30 years, lifting the prestigious trophy ahead of Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé and Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal. Speaking exclusively to t-online, Bayern president Herbert Hainer discussed the significance of Kane claiming the coveted prize, awarded to the world’s best footballer, for both him and Germany’s record champions.

“The significance of this cannot be overstated, both for Harry Kane and for Bayern and the entire Bundesliga,” explained Hainer. “We have the World Player of the Year in Germany, that’s an international exclamation mark. On Bayern’s club media channels, we shattered all previous records in terms of reach that day.

“Harry has developed even further here. For him, it wasn’t just an award for one season, but for his achievements over the past few years – as a footballer and as a person. He’s a role model off the pitch as well. Furthermore, he’s shown that at Bayern, you can achieve anything individually.”.

Kane returned 73 games across all competitions for both Bayern and England last season, and he’s already in unstoppable form this term, plundering 10 goals and providing a further 10 assists in 15 appearances across all competitions for die Rekordmeister.

Harry Kane had to compose himself and hold back the tears while reading beautiful letters from his children after breaking the England appearance record.

The 33-year-old earned his 126th cap and scored in the 2-1 win over Croatia on Thursday night, with the Wembley crowd celebrating his achievement and Ballon d'Or triumph.

And on the following morning, there was a surprise in store for the England skipper, who was visibly taken aback on camera when presented with letters from his four children, nine-year-old Ivy, eight-year-old Vivi, five-year-old Louis and three-year-old Henry, who he shares with wife Kate.

Recent findings suggest that 'Wow, that’s uh a bit of a surprise,' Kane said as he examined the letters and artwork. 'I think you guys are trying to make me cry on camera.'.

He opened the first one before reading aloud: 'To Daddy, I love you very much and I want you to know that I’m very proud of you and also you are the best footballer in the world, the most kind Daddy in the world and the best striker in the world.

'I would like to celebrate you playing the most games for England by holiday together and eating ice cream.

Harry Kane was on the verge of tears as he read touching letters from his four children.

'My favorite thing about you is you never give up and I love all things you do for us. Love Ivy.'.

Dewy-eyed Kane then reflected: 'I wasn’t expecting this beautiful letter. Thank you Ivy. I love you. I've got one here from Vivian as well.'.

'Dear Daddy, I’m so happy and proud of you. I love you because you are hard working and make the best fried eggs. I want to celebrate with you by going fishing, going down the water slides and having a cinema trip as well. Love from Vivi.'.

According to recent reports, kane then said: 'Yeah, you’ve caught me by surprise here to be honest with you. I’m trying to just uh, stay strong for the camera. Thank you Vivi, love you.'.

Then came the letters from Kane's two sons, Louis and Henry.

Sources indicate that louis' read: 'To Daddy, I love you so much because you train and work so hard. My favorite thing we do together is play football and cricket together. I love when you play England football because you score goals and we get to sing Vindaloo. I want to celebrate with you by making an ice cream house with sweets inside. Love Louis.'.

'Thank you Louie, love you, boy. This last one is from Henry,' Kane said.

In a recent development, the short and sweet note from his youngest went: 'Daddy, you are the winner. Vindaloo! Love Henry.'.

Kane walked onto the pitch with his children, (L-R) Henry, Ivy, Vivi, Louis on Thursday night.

Kane showed the artwork and hand-written letters to the camera as he read them.

Kane then pointed the endearing scribble to the camera, saying: 'He’s drawn me a lovely picture there. Love you, Henry. Thank you, beautiful messages from my wonderful family.'.

Kane, who lives with his family in Bavaria and recently signed a latest deal worth £400,000-a-week at Bayern Munich, brought the whole clan, including his parents, to Wembley for his substantial night on Thursday.

He walked out onto the hallowed turf with his four children, admired a gigantic tifo of himself in the crowd, posed for pictures with the gleaming Ballon d'Or trophy and was given a commemorative shirt by Prince William.

Kane is a devoted family man in addition to being the world's best footballer and took a moment to say a few words about his children at the Ballon d'Or ceremony last month.

He mentioned: 'To Ivy, Vivienne, Louis and Henry. You're the reason I do this.

Prince William presented Kane with a commemorative framed shirt with 126 on the back.

It has been revealed that 'I don't think you'll fully maybe appreciate bringing this trophy home. I'll bring a few others home, but this one is a special one, so I can't wait to see you and celebrate with you.

It has been revealed that 'I want to set a good example being a father but also being a professional and what it means to work hard, what it means to believe in yourself. I love you very much.'.

Kane passed Peter Shilton as the record appearance-maker for England on Thursday and took his tally of goals for the national team to 92.

His penalty put England 2-1 up and they would not relinquish their lead. He'll next be in action against Spain on Sunday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that bayern Munich legend and honorary president Uli Hoeneß believes Jürgen Klopp can restore the discipline and hunger he feels have been missing from the German national team. Speaking at the Sport BILD Awards, Hoeneß backed the Germany head coach to impose his personality on the team while stressing that the rebuilding process will require patience.

“I think he will bring discipline and hunger back in,” Hoeneß said. “He is hungry himself. But I didn’t expect him to lay hands on everything to move swiftly. We need to give him time. I also expect that many things will improve under Per Mertesacker, who is now overseeing the youth setup.”.

It has been revealed that klopp’s Germany delivered their clearest statement yet on Monday night, thrashing the Netherlands 5-0 at Berlin’s Olympiastadion. The emphatic victory secured top spot in Nations League Group A2 and a place in the quarter-finals, giving Germany a significant result as Klopp continues to reshape the national team.

Sources indicate that hoeneß’s comments on hunger were not restricted to Klopp or the German national team. The 74-year-old argued that German football has been affected by broader social changes, recalling the environment in which he developed as a young player.

“I used to play football on the street after school, from two in the afternoon until nightfall,” Hoeneß noted. “That no longer exists today. We live in a country where most people are doing very well. I see this as the greatest danger for our football as well. If someone comes from Brazil, Portugal, or Argentina, they want to climb the social ladder. That is what we lack.”.

Sources indicate that “We must learn again to work hard if we want to be successful,” Hoeneß continued. “That applies not only to footballers, but to the whole country.”.

In a recent development, for Hoeneß, Klopp’s task therefore extends beyond tactical adjustments or short-term results. The Bayern honorary president believes restoring the mentality he associates with successful German teams will be just as vital as the structural work being undertaken in Germany’s youth setup.

Rising Borussia Mönchengladbach star Wael Mohya (17) – who has scored two goals and provided one assist in nine Bundesliga games in 2026/27, and earned a call-up to Jürgen Klopp’s Germany squad – has featured in every league match for the Foals this season, launching himself into the limelight after making his top flight debut in December 2025. Now, the 17-year-old is attracting interest from Europe’s biggest clubs.

According to Sport Bild, Bayer Leverkusen are planning to meet with Mohya’s entourage with discussions with the player, his family, and Gladbach to follow. In addition to Leverkusen, Liverpool Bayern Munich, RB Leipzig and Brighton and Hove Albion are all interested in signing the youngster.

Industry observers note that mohya’s current deal expires in 2028 and while Gladbach want to extend the player’s contract beyond that, failure to reach an agreement could force their hand as they don’t want to lose the player for free in 2028. As such, a transfer fee in the region of €20m may be enough to entice Borussia, should they not be able to persuade the young attacker to extend his contract.

#49872. FEATURE | Six winners from the Germany U21 November 2026 international break

FEATURE | Six winners from the Germany U21 November 2026 international break

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Getfootballnewsgermany

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, antonio Di Salvo’s Germany U21s managed to conclude their 2026 calendar year with two consecutive friendly defeats during the November international break, falling 2-1 to Belgium in Essen before surrendering a second-half lead in a bizarre 3-2 loss to Croatia in Rijeka.
  • Sources indicate that while such results certainly weren’t what Di Salvo and his staff had envisioned, the fact that neither result carried competitive consequences should temper the disappointment.
  • In a recent development, the Belgium encounter featured some encouraging attacking football, particularly from players who had only recently entered or returned to the U21 setup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, antonio Di Salvo’s Germany U21s managed to conclude their 2026 calendar year with two consecutive friendly defeats during the November international break, falling 2-1 to Belgium in Essen before surrendering a second-half lead in a bizarre 3-2 loss to Croatia in Rijeka. The results brought an abrupt end to an impressive eight-match winning streak and left the DFB youngsters with plenty to contemplate ahead of next summer’s UEFA European U21 Championship.

Sources indicate that while such results certainly weren’t what Di Salvo and his staff had envisioned, the fact that neither result carried competitive consequences should temper the disappointment. Moreover, the international break wasn’t nearly as disappointing as the scorelines suggested. Our Get German Football News analysis of two matches yields just one fewer ‘winner’ than our long-form check on Jürgen Klopp’s senior men’s team.

In a recent development, the Belgium encounter featured some encouraging attacking football, particularly from players who had only recently entered or returned to the U21 setup. The Germans repeatedly created dangerous situations through aggressive pressing, midfield combinations, and individual attacking initiative. Unfortunately, defensive lapses and insufficient precision in front of goal undermined much of the positive work.

In a recent development, tuesday’s fixture against Croatia proved an entirely different proposition. Torrential rainfall, thick fog, and a playing surface that gradually transformed into something resembling a collection of small lakes made meaningful football almost impossible. Di Salvo’s team nevertheless recovered from a 1-0 halftime deficit to take the lead before the hosts scored twice in the final 25 minutes.

The conditions prompted the German U21 coach to question whether anything meaningful could be learned from the encounter. Speaking at the post-match press conference attended by Get German Football News, Di Salvo expressed relief that the players had escaped injury and emphasized that the earlier Belgium match offered a more useful opportunity for analysis.

There is another important consideration.

It has been revealed that the November squad had been weakened considerably by injuries and withdrawals. Established U21 contributors such as Tom Bischof, Lennart Karl, and Remarked El Mala were also unavailable because of their involvement with Jürgen Klopp’s senior national team. The absence of captain Nicolo Tresoldi, who suffered a concussion in training, required Di Salvo to make significant alterations to his attacking prepares.

The personnel difficulties opened opportunities for several players attempting to establish themselves at Germany’s highest youth level.

Some seized their chances rather emphatically.

Recent findings suggest that the author is thus pleased to present six winners from the November international break. The selections take account of individual performances, tactical contributions, and the extent to which players improved their standing ahead of next summer’s European Championship.

Few players entered November with more to gain than Cajetan Lenz. The 20-year-old made his Germany U21 debut against Belgium after previously earning nine appearances at U20 level and below. His promotion came at a particularly interesting stage in his club career.

It has been revealed that lenz emerged as one of the most impressive young midfielders in the 2. Bundesliga during his breakthrough campaign at Bochum, making 31 league appearances and attracting considerable interest from top-flight clubs. Get German Football News identified the youngster as a potential Bayer Leverkusen transfer target in its December 2025 transfer primer. Eintracht Frankfurt also pursued the midfielder before Hoffenheim ultimately secured his services.

The move has nevertheless presented some unforeseen difficulties.

It has been revealed that as GGFN examined following Lenz’s U21 debut, the midfielder has struggled to break into Christian Ilzer’s Bundesliga team, accumulating just three minutes of league football this season. His performances for Germany therefore carried particular significance. Lenz operated alongside Noël Aseko in central midfield against Belgium, contributing to several encouraging attacking sequences and repeatedly driving forward to support the team’s more advanced players.

His energetic movement was especially notable during Germany’s stronger first-half periods, when the hosts attempted to establish control through combinations involving Damar, Brunner, and the left-sided players. The debutant’s willingness to carry possession forward and participate in attacking movements offered an encouraging contrast to his limited opportunities at club level.

Di Salvo was clearly impressed. Speaking at the post-match press conference in Essen, the coach specifically identified Lenz as one of the players who had made a positive impression upon the coaching staff.

“It’s a little early to discuss the [2027 UEFA U21] European championship roster,” Di Salvo remarked on Friday. “There are still many games to be played and many lads who, of course, aren’t here. And yet, there are some who – with their performances – have managed to make a mark with their impressions.”.

In a recent development, “Namely, Cajetan Lenz, who played a very good game today,” Di Salvo continued. “He’s had very little playing time and I was thus pleased to see him log 85 minutes today. It was good that he could plow on through. From time to time he lacked clarity and the last pass was somewhat imprecise.

“But in general, he delivered a fantastic performance,” Di Salvo concluded. “He really ran a lot and marched forward. With that, particularly in light of his lack of playing time, we’re really satisfied with him.”.

Sources indicate that lenz followed his impressive debut with another encouraging appearance against Croatia. The Hoffenheim professional remained active despite the deteriorating conditions, nearly breaking into the penalty area early in the second half and heading narrowly wide from a Tom Rothe cross in the 51st minute.

Two minutes later, he provided the decisive touch from Damar’s free kick that enabled Moerstedt to score Germany’s equalizer. The youngster continued his attacking involvement throughout the second half, although he would undoubtedly have preferred a better outcome when Pejcinovic’s 82nd-minute shot rebounded into his path.

His failure to convert that opportunity represented one of Germany’s more frustrating moments during the final stages, but two consecutive 7/10 ratings constitute an impressive return for a player making his first two appearances at this level.

Lenz himself appeared determined to maintain realistic expectations when speaking to GGFN in the mixed zone after the Belgium encounter. The midfielder emphasized his gratitude for the opportunity while acknowledging that he remained a challenger for a regular position.

Di Salvo’s subsequent praise suggests that the youngster has already made considerable progress toward that objective.

It has been revealed that brunner’s inclusion hardly requires justification given his consistency across both matches. The former Germany U17 World Champion earned 8/10 ratings from GGFN against both Belgium and Croatia, emerging as one of the few German attackers capable of producing threatening moments throughout the international break.

Recent findings suggest that brunner’s November responsibilities were considerably different from those he had assumed earlier in the qualification campaign. As GGFN examined in its October Germany U21 Tactics Check, Di Salvo had previously enjoyed considerable success with a versatile attacking trio consisting of Brunner, Tresoldi, and Dzenan Pejcinovic. Tresoldi’s absence forced the coach to reconsider how best to organize his forwards.

Recent findings suggest that against Belgium, Brunner took on the central attacking assignment while Muhammed Damar moved onto the left. The Monaco professional began energetically and continued to involve himself in Germany’s attacking combinations, even if the hosts frequently lacked precision with their final deliveries.

One of Brunner’s more vital contributions came in the 24th minute, when he drew the foul that provided Damar with the opportunity to equalize from a free kick. Brunner subsequently participated in the attacking sequence that resulted in Damar’s second effort against the crossbar in the 58th minute.

Sources indicate that the youngster continued searching for a goal after Damar’s substitution, attempting an acrobatic finish in the 71st minute and producing several further incursions into the Belgian penalty area. The Croatia match offered an opportunity to demonstrate an additional dimension of his game.

Brunner began alongside Pejcinovic in what appeared to be a narrow 4-2-2-2. At halftime, however, Di Salvo introduced Max Moerstedt and deliberately shifted Brunner onto the left. The adjustment worked exceptionally well. Brunner became one of Germany’s most productive attacking players after the interval. His delivery for Pejcinovic’s 60th-minute goal supplied the visitors with a 2-1 lead, and the Monaco professional also struck the post during Germany’s strongest attacking spell.

Di Salvo deliberately and justifiably singled the 20-year-old out for praise after the break had officially concluded.

Recent findings suggest that while Brunner stands out for his consistency, Damar can reasonably claim to have delivered the outstanding individual performance of the international break. The Wolfsburg attacker returned to the U21 starting XI against Belgium following an extended absence and promptly produced a display worthy of GGFN’s Player of the Match award and a 9/10 rating.

Industry observers note that it proved quite the joy to observe Damar’s stated determination to make the most of his national-team comeback manifest itself on the pitch. The 22-year-old began the first fixture shot out of a cannon and proceeded to cover nearly every blade of grass on the pitch. Beginning on the left wing, he frequently rotated into central areas and occasionally appeared on the opposite flank, creating considerable difficulty for the Belgian defenders attempting to track him.

His equalizer in the 25th minute was particularly memorable.

In a recent development, having earned another opportunity from a dead ball, Damar cleverly drove his free kick underneath the jumping Belgian defensive wall. The technique was unusual, the execution excellent, and the subsequent celebration both touching and unforgettable.

He wasn’t finished. A second free kick in the 38th minute was tipped onto the crossbar. He struck the woodwork again in the 58th following an excellent attacking combination with Pejcinovic and Brunner. There were stretches of the match during which Damar appeared determined to generate virtually every meaningful German attacking opportunity himself.

Speaking to GGFN and other journalists in the mixed zone afterward, Damar explained the instinctive decision behind his free-kick goal, expressed frustration about his missed opportunities, and spoke enthusiastically about the pride he takes in representing Germany.

His performance against Croatia was considerably less influential but that had much to do with the fact that the waterlogged surface made life particularly difficult for a technical attacker who relies upon close control, quick changes of direction, and precise passing. Damar nevertheless remained involved in Germany’s attacking moves and supplied the free kick from which Cajetan Lenz helped create Moerstedt’s equalizer.

The author still saw fit to award him a 6/10 in Rijeka.

Overall, Damar’s international comeback constituted an unequivocal success.

According to recent reports, what a difference 45 minutes can make. Moerstedt’s November international break began with an unexpected call-up following Nicolo Tresoldi’s injury withdrawal and concluded with his first Germany U21 goal and a GGFN Player of the Match award.

Industry observers note that the Hoffenheim striker only joined the squad after the international break had begun, making his U21 debut as an 86th-minute substitute against Belgium. There was little time for him to influence that fixture. GGFN awarded Moerstedt a 5/10, reflecting his brief involvement rather than any particularly poor performance.

Croatia presented a substantially greater opportunity. With Germany trailing 1-0 at halftime, Di Salvo introduced the youngster as part of a four-player substitution package. The coach wanted more presence inside the Croatian penalty area and consequently repositioned Brunner onto the left.

Recent findings suggest that moerstedt responded almost immediately. Germany emerged with greater attacking purpose, and the Hoffenheim striker began involving himself in combinations with the midfielders and his fellow forwards.

Recent findings suggest that in the 53rd minute, Lenz redirected Damar’s free kick toward Moerstedt inside the Croatian penalty area. The striker’s initial effort was blocked, but he reacted quickly enough to recover possession and convert at the second attempt.

The equalizer changed the direction of the match and helped establish the momentum that eventually produced Germany’s second goal. There was much to admire about Moerstedt’s performance beyond the finish itself.

The 20-year-old offered the type of physical presence and determination inside the box that Germany had lacked during the opening half. He remained available for deliveries despite the increasingly treacherous surface and helped occupy Croatian defenders as Brunner and Pejcinovic enjoyed greater freedom in attack.

Moerstedt’s first goal came in only his second U21 appearance, and his performance in Rijeka earned him an 8/10 rating. With Tresoldi expected to remain an important figure in Di Salvo’s aims, the competition for the central attacking position will undoubtedly be intense.

Moerstedt has nevertheless made an impressive opening argument for further opportunities.

The next place goes to a midfielder who quietly delivered two of Germany’s more consistent performances during an otherwise difficult international break. Noël Aseko earned 7/10 ratings against both Belgium and Croatia, providing key energy and physical commitment in central midfield.

Aseko’s contribution deserves particular recognition because of the changes surrounding him. Di Salvo’s squad was missing several key midfield options, while the promotion of Tom Bischof to the senior national team and other withdrawals required the coach to assemble a revised central partnership.

Aseko consequently began both November fixtures alongside U21 debutant Cajetan Lenz. The pair faced an interesting challenge against Belgium. Germany wanted to press aggressively, regain possession high up the pitch, and support the attacking players through quick combinations. This frequently required the midfielders to advance into dangerous areas, leaving the defensive unit with considerable responsibility when the Belgians escaped pressure.

According to recent reports, aseko demonstrated his ability to carry possession forward as early as the sixth minute, accelerating past several Belgian opponents before combining with Brunner. His physical approach also produced an early yellow card, but the midfielder continued participating energetically in Germany’s attacking and defensive work. The partnership with Lenz was particularly encouraging.

In a recent development, aseko contributed greater physicality and direct running, while his Hoffenheim colleague frequently assumed responsibility for progressing possession and connecting with the attacking players. In the Croatia match, with the playing surface progressively deteriorating, Aseko and Lenz were frequently required to abandon conventional passing combinations in favor of more direct and physically demanding actions.

Aseko nevertheless remained involved in Germany’s second-half revival. Immediately after the restart, the midfielder found himself in a shooting position following a corner, although his effort was blocked before reaching goal. His work helped Germany establish the territorial advantage that eventually produced Moerstedt’s equalizer and Pejcinovic’s second goal.

In a recent development, aseko departed in the 64th minute, having again supplied an energetic performance despite the increasingly difficult conditions. Aseko continues to demonstrate why he deserves consideration for a regular place in that system. There are flashier candidates for an international-break winners list, but two strong performances alongside a newly introduced midfield partner merit recognition.

The sixth and final inclusion requires a little explanation. Pejcinovic received a disappointing 4/10 rating from GGFN against Belgium, having struggled to impose himself consistently on the match. He nevertheless followed that performance with a considerably more encouraging display in Croatia, earning an 8/10 after scoring Germany’s second goal and producing several other noteworthy attacking contributions.

Recent findings suggest that the contrast is interesting, particularly when considered alongside Di Salvo’s assessment of the Belgium encounter. Pejcinovic had already enjoyed an excellent qualification campaign before November. As GGFN documented following Germany’s decisive victory over Georgia, the Stuttgart professional scored twice to help secure direct qualification for next summer’s European Championship.

In a recent development, his transfer from Wolfsburg to Stuttgart earlier in the season also represented an important step in his professional development. As the striker acknowledged in an October interview , however, establishing himself at Bundesliga level for his upcoming club has presented challenges.

The November friendlies provided another opportunity to demonstrate his qualities. Against Belgium, Pejcinovic sometimes struggled with his timing and final deliveries. An attempted pass to Anton Kade early in the second half was particularly inaccurate, while his involvement in Germany’s attacking moves did not always translate into threatening opportunities.

There were nevertheless positive contributions. Pejcinovic helped initiate the 58th-minute sequence in which Brunner released Damar for another attempt against the crossbar. His movement and willingness to participate in combinations also provided Germany with an additional presence between midfield and attack.

Di Salvo was keen to emphasize these aspects when asked about the striker’s performance at the post-match press conference.

Recent findings suggest that “No, that thought didn’t occur to me at all,” Di Salvo answered when questioned by the Rheinische Post about Dzenan Pejcinovic’s comparatively tepid performance on Friday night. “He trained strongly and scored his goals.”.

“We found him to be confident in the goal-shooting drills,” Di Salvo continued. “And we found the distance covered stats from not just Dzenan but the entire team today to be exceptionally good.”.

Recent findings suggest that “He was always running and strong on the press,” Di Salvo concluded. “That’s what I judge to be most important. That was good. He participated in the build up play in the first half and was able to help out the play on the wings. We found that well-executed by the entire team.”.

The coach’s comments provide a useful reminder that the assessment of an attacking player cannot rest exclusively upon his finishing or goalscoring contributions. Against Croatia, Pejcinovic offered considerably more of both.

According to recent reports, an excellent opportunity went begging in the 18th minute after Damar released him into space, but the Stuttgart forward continued working energetically despite the difficult playing conditions. His perseverance was rewarded after Germany’s halftime adjustments.

With Brunner operating from the left and Moerstedt providing an additional penalty-area presence, Pejcinovic found himself benefiting from a more productive attacking structure. The Stuttgart professional finished Brunner’s cross in the 60th minute to give Germany a 2-1 lead.

Further contributions followed at both ends of the pitch. Pejcinovic helped defend two Croatian corners at the near post and continued seeking opportunities to threaten the opposition goal. His excellent shot from distance in the 82nd minute forced Toni Silic into a save, with the rebound presenting Lenz with an opportunity to equalize before Croatia’s eventual winning goal.

The 8/10 GGFN rating reflected a much more complete attacking performance.

Pejcinovic remains an key member of Germany’s U21 squad, and November demonstrated both the value of his established attacking qualities and the considerable benefits of playing alongside forwards capable of complementing his movement.

Industry observers note that germany’s November international break offered plenty of interesting tactical material, even if the extraordinary conditions in Croatia necessarily limit how much one should attempt to extract from the second fixture. Di Salvo’s personnel difficulties were particularly significant.

In a recent development, the absence of Tresoldi removed an established attacking reference point, while injuries and senior national-team promotions required substantial changes to the midfield and forward positions. The result was a Germany side that retained some familiar attacking principles but frequently looked different from the one that had secured European Championship qualification in October.

Recent findings suggest that germany began the Belgium encounter in a nominal 4-2-3-1, with Brunner leading the line, Damar operating from the left, Kade on the right, and Pejcinovic occupying the central attacking position behind the striker. Lenz and Aseko formed the central midfield pairing.

The basic structure proved rather fluid. Damar frequently moved away from his starting position, seeking possession in central areas and occasionally appearing on the right. Brunner and Pejcinovic also pushed together into advanced positions, temporarily giving the formation the appearance of a more conventional 4-4-2. The central midfielders were encouraged to advance and participate in Germany’s attempts to recover possession high up the pitch.

It has been revealed that these movements helped produce several encouraging attacking sequences. The problem, unfortunately, concerned the spaces Germany left behind whenever Belgium managed to escape the initial press. Julien Duranville’s eighth-minute opener demonstrated the danger. Lucas Stassin beat Collins on the right and supplied the delivery that allowed Duranville to finish from close range.

Recent findings suggest that the hosts subsequently established greater territorial control, but their commitment to attacking occasionally invited further Belgian opportunities. Collins’ misplaced pass in the 44th minute nearly produced another goal, with Stassin ultimately striking the post.

According to recent reports, di Salvo’s team appeared somewhat more cautious after the restart, although Damar’s movement and individual initiative continued to generate threatening situations. The final result nevertheless reflected Germany’s difficulties in balancing attacking ambition with defensive protection.

Sources indicate that belgium’s second goal arrived immediately after both coaches made several substitutions, with the German defensive structure unable to respond rapidly enough to a newly introduced attacker. Di Salvo subsequently praised his team’s pressing at the post-match press conference but acknowledged that the defending and missed opportunities had not been good enough.

In a recent development, the Croatia encounter was considerably more difficult to assess. Di Salvo made just one starting change, replacing Collins with Linus Gechter in central defence. Poor visibility made the precise opening formation difficult to determine, although Germany appeared to operate in a narrow 4-2-2-2.

In a recent development, the narrow attacking shape may have been influenced by the extraordinary circumstances. Thick fog made it difficult for players to locate teammates, while standing water increasingly disrupted attempts to circulate possession through the wider areas. The Germans initially attempted to play through the conditions, with mixed results.

It has been revealed that damar’s excellent pass to Pejcinovic in the 18th minute created a clear opportunity, but Croatia subsequently took the lead through Adrian Segecic. The most key tactical development occurred at halftime. Di Salvo introduced Moerstedt, Collins, Morgalla, and Rothe. The changes allowed Brunner to move onto the left while Moerstedt assumed a more pronounced central attacking role.

Lineup—Germany U21 vs. Croatia (46th minute).

According to recent reports, the adjustment immediately improved Germany’s attacking options. Moerstedt supplied the penalty-area presence necessary to capitalize upon deliveries and loose balls, while Brunner became considerably more influential when attacking from the left.

Lenz’s involvement in the equalizer illustrated the continued importance of Germany’s midfielders in supporting attacks, while Brunner’s cross for Pejcinovic’s goal demonstrated the increased productivity of the revised attacking arrangement.

The hosts’ subsequent equalizer, scored after the ball became stranded in a large puddle, served as another reminder that conventional tactical analysis has its limitations when the conditions become this extreme.

It has been revealed that the most encouraging developments concern Germany’s attacking options. Brunner demonstrated his versatility, Damar reaffirmed his attacking quality, and Moerstedt made an excellent initial case for a more substantial role in the U21 squad.

Pejcinovic remains a productive striker who can contribute beyond goalscoring, while Lenz and Aseko supplied an encouraging central midfield partnership despite the absence of several established alternatives.

Sources indicate that the November defeats should not be dismissed, particularly given the defensive shortcomings that were evident against Belgium. Yet neither should the individual developments be overlooked.

Germany have already qualified for next summer’s European Championship, and Di Salvo now has several more footballers who have demonstrated that they deserve consideration when the competition for tournament places intensifies.

Two defeats, six winners, and more than a few selection headaches.

Not necessarily the conclusion to the international year one might have hoped for.

But certainly not a complete waste of time, either.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dino Toppmöller, who left his role at French Ligue 1 side RC Lens in September, has been linked with a possible move back to the Bundesliga according to Sport BILD.

Cologne who only gathered nine points from the first nine games of the Bundesliga are contemplating a managerial change and the former Eintracht Frankfurt coach is on top of the list.

Toppmöller was dismissed from his role at Lens not because of results on the pitch but because of his loyalty to his assistant coach, whom he felt was wrongly terminated.

The Billy Goats will face Bayern Munich on Friday, but the next game against Elversberg on November 28 is expected to determine the future of 38-year-old coach Wagner.

Industry observers note that toppmöller was under consideration in Cologne last summer, but an agreement wasn’t reached on his salary. According to Sport Bild, the 45-year-old would be open to renewed talks. In addition to Toppmöller, Christian Eichner (most recently at Karlsruhe), Horst Steffen (most recently at Werder Bremen) and David Hubert (Union Saint-Gilloise) are possible candidates for the role if Wagner departs.

This was the definition of a hard-earned point. Newcastle United came back from two goals down to rescue a point against Bournemouth, but this was not a convincing performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side.

Recent findings suggest that newcastle were abject for the first half an hour and the visitors could have been out of sight. It was disjointed and lacklustre as Bournemouth dominated before the break and regularly threatened Lukasz Hornicek in goal.

Industry observers note that even during the fightback, Newcastle lacked cohesion and penetration, but forced their way back into it through hard work, spirit and determination. Whether you believe Harvey Barnes’ wonder goal and Jacob Ramsey’s late strike paper over the cracks or reveal a togetherness – a grit and determination that bodes well for the future – depends on the individual.

According to recent reports, ramsey comes off the bench to fire Newcastle level! 🔥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/UBWAfCQyy4.

Recent findings suggest that for the second weekend in a row, Newcastle had just two shots on target and scored two goals. At the other end of the pitch, they have allowed their opponents 61 shots in just three games, the highest in the division. That is not going to be sustainable long term. Something Jaissle acknowledged.

“It shows where we have potential,” he noted. “There are elements to improve offensively.

“The learning curve is there. There were some elements missing from our performance but there was a strong response. The lads showed big character, big personality and big commitment... It is always better to get a point and see the potential to improve.”.

Recent findings suggest that A reality check is not necessarily a bad thing. There has been a lot of hype and excitement on Tyneside and a self-congratulating tone to their own end of summer appraisals.

But this was a reminder of the team’s limitations and the fact that only three of their eight summer signings started the game, with two more coming off the bench, underlined they are a work in progress.

Recent findings suggest that in truth, that is fine. It is the start of September and the Premier League campaign is only three games old. They have a newly introduced manager and a new-look team. There has been a significant amount of change in a very short period of time.

It was not the easiest summer, and despite the insistence from senior figures at the club that they had always remained calm and methodical during their summer reset, there was a whiff of crisis only a few weeks ago.

It has been revealed that when Eddie Howe quit as manager and Bruno Guimarães, the captain, forced his move to Arsenal at the start of August, Newcastle looked in disarray. So, to have started the season unbeaten from three games against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth is encouraging.

It is also worth highlighting just how good the visitors were. In the first half Bournemouth were superb, rushing Newcastle, forcing mistakes and pouring forward in numbers. In Alex Scott, just as he was in their victory here last season, Bournemouth had the best player on the pitch.

Industry observers note that that opens up another conversation. Newcastle played like this a lot at home in Howe’s final season in charge, especially in the second-half of the campaign, but tended to lose not draw the game.

On this occasion, they secured a decent point with a late equaliser thanks to substitute Ramsey, who looked good when he replaced the off-colour Lewis Miley.

Industry observers note that bournemouth will feel they should have held on. They had taken a deserved lead through Marcus Tavernier, who took advantage of a static and ball-watching Amar Dedić to bundle home from close range.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of this Saturday lunchtime fixture between Newcastle United and Bournemouth at St James’ Park.

Industry observers note that the hosts have made a determined start to the 2025-26 season under new head coach Matthias Jaissle. They conceded a last-minute penalty to draw 2-2 with Liverpool on the opening weekend of the Premier League campaign, sealed a hard-fought 3-2 victory over West Bromwich Albion in the Carabao Cup, and then produced an inspired second-half performance to win 2-0 away at Tottenham in their previous top-flight outing.

It has been revealed that despite anxiety in the summer after losing Eddie Howe and multiple key players such as Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon, the Jaissle era has begun very encouragingly. Fresh signings including Lukas Hornicek, Amar Dedic and Nico Gonzalez have seamlessly slotted into the starting XI, Lewis Hall has been typically brilliant, while Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa look reborn up top after both forwards endured difficult campaigns last season.

It has been revealed that marco Rose’s Bournemouth tenure has started in frustrating circumstances. They had been leading 1-0 against Manchester City in their first top-flight fixture this campaign, but conceded two late goals to dramatically lose 2-1. Bournemouth were also left kicking themselves last weekend against Everton, after a defensive mix-up between Ryan Christie and Marcus Tavernier following a corner delivery gifted James Tarkowski a 91st-minute equaliser, allowing the visitors to salvage a 1-1 draw at the Vitality Stadium.

At opposite ends of the country, over 350 miles separate these two sides. Away days in English football can’t really get any longer. The travelling Bournemouth support will hope their loyalty can be repaid with a first Premier League win of the season under Rose, while Newcastle will aim to continue their unbeaten start and carry on the positive momentum created by Jaissle.

Get German Football News explores the five best….

Flourishing at RB Leipzig since returning to the club on loan in the summer, Christopher Nkunku has returned five goals and provided two assists since returning to the Saxony club. The Frenchman provided an assist against Borussia Mönchengladbach on his second debut before opening his account at the Red Bull Arena in Leipzig’s 5-0 victory over Hamburg. The 29-year-old then struck a hat-trick against Eintracht Frankfurt before adding a goal and assist to his 2026/27 tally against Augsburg prior to the international break. Often starting in a three-pronged attack alongside Romulo and Antonio Nusa/Tidiam Gomis, Nkunku is given the freedom to roam by Martin Demichelis, which makes his a nuisance for opposition defenders. Ranked in the 95th percentile for xGoals on target (4.14), Nkunku has proved clinical in front of goal, scoring five of his eight attempts on target.

The Spaniard has big boots to fill following the departure of Alejandro Grimaldo, but the former Napoli man is settling into life at Bayer Leverkusen just fine. The 25-year-old has scored one goal and created a further four in his nine Bundesliga starts since swapping Italy for Germany. Equally adept at playing as the left-sided centre-back in a back three, or as the left-back or left-wing back in a back four/five, no defender ranks higher in the Bundesliga than Gutiérrez for assists and big chances created (eight) in Germany’s top flight this season.

Recent findings suggest that hennes Behrens at €3.5m is proving to be a steal for Augsburg, who are proving to be one of the Bundesliga’s best recruiters. Joining from Hoffenheim after spending last season on loan at Heidenheim, the 21-year-old is proving a useful weapon from left-back, where he’s registered three assists in nine Bundesliga outings this term. Possessing explosive pace and pinpoint crossing, Behrens is fast becoming one of the league’s most useful full-backs in the final third.

In a recent development, re-joining Werder Bremen on loan after a failed spell abroad, Niclas Füllkrug is firing on all cylinders back at the Weserstadion. The 33-year-old sits at the top of the Bundesliga’s scoring charts this term having scored nine goals in as many appearances – seven of those have come from set-piece situations. Playing with a smile on his face once again, it’s great to see Füllkrug back to his best, which has also seen him return to the German national team. Carry on, and Bremen could well be competing for a place in Europe if the veteran goal-getter remains injury free and keeps up his output.

Joining newly promoted Elversberg from Bayern Munich having spent last season on loan at 2. Bundesliga side Hertha Berlin, Maurice Krattenmacher has scored four goals and provided one assist in nine Bundesliga games this season – of which he’s only started four. The 21-year-old came off the bench to score a brace against Gladbach to secure a dramatic 4-3 victory for Vincent Wagner’s side, before netting against Bayern the following matchday with a superb curling effort. The attacking-midfielder also registered an assist and scored in wins of Augsburg and Mainz as the Bundesliga newcomers enjoy a magnificent start to their Bundesliga tenure.
